performers: Alisa Weilerstein, cello; Jason Yoder, marimba
intro: Alisa Weilerstein plays The Swan at the White House with a sixteen-year-old marimba player, Jason Yoder. His mallets give the rippling accompaniment a wooden glow beneath her bowed melody.

sections.label: B · The melody climbs and turns
sections.mNote: The cello’s long notes span the marimba’s separate strokes

sections.label: C · The cello’s broad phrases
sections.mNote: The marimba keeps the broken chords moving

cues.title: A bow and wooden bars
cues.text: Saint-Saëns gives the cello a long melody over almost ceaseless broken chords. Here those chords belong to a marimba. Yoder strikes its wooden bars with mallets while Weilerstein draws out the cello line: two very different ways of keeping a phrase alive.
cues.evidence: The official White House video shows Yoder playing marimba beside Weilerstein on 4 November 2009: https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/alisa-weilerstein-and-jason-yoder-perform-white-house-5-8. The original cello melody and accompaniment are in Durand score D.S. 3891.

cues.title: Sixteen at the White House
cues.text: Jason Yoder is sixteen when he joins Weilerstein for the White House’s Evening of Classical Music. The familiar cello solo becomes a duet between a touring soloist and a young percussionist, sharing the stage in Washington.
cues.evidence: The official White House description names cellist Alisa Weilerstein and sixteen-year-old percussionist Jason Yoder, and dates the event to 4 November 2009: https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/alisa-weilerstein-and-jason-yoder-perform-white-house-5-8

cues.title: The bow comes to rest
cues.text: In the closing bars, the cello’s melody slows and settles on a high G. The accompaniment continues under the held note and outlasts it. Saint-Saëns gives the soloist a long silence at the end, while the last broken chords complete the phrase.
cues.evidence: Durand score, plate D.S. 3891, p. 3, final five bars; Carl Fischer cello part (1907), final line. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5f/IMSLP925269-PMLP06099-2024-03-15-12-42-19-01.PDF
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: A pianist at ten and an organist for twenty years, he wrote the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons with a xylophone, and a zoo he forbade anyone to print.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. Two widows raised the sickly boy: his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before the next. By his own account he already listened to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, a “microscopic oboe” that swelled until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, with the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
